hook: Nurses: why does a racing heart lose its pulse?
hook_backups: Nurses: heart rate 180. Pumping more, or less?
Nurses: wide and fast on the monitor. What first?

memory_line: Ventricular tachycardia (RACE): too fast to fill. Pulse first.
caption_lesson:
✅ First, normal sinus rhythm
• The SA (sinoatrial) node leads. The ventricles fire together down the fast wiring (narrow QRS) and refill between beats

〰️ Then ventricular tachycardia (RACE)
1️⃣ A spot in the ventricles (lower chambers) takes over and fires fast, often 150 to 250 a minute. The SA node gets ignored
2️⃣ The beat starts in the wrong place and spreads slowly, muscle to muscle, so every QRS is wide (0.12 seconds or more)
3️⃣ The ventricles RACE: too fast to fill, so each squeeze pushes less blood and the BP (blood pressure) can crash
4️⃣ It can lose its pulse or turn into ventricular fibrillation (QUIVER) with little warning

⚡ Pulse first, then decide
• Check the carotid (neck) pulse, 10 seconds or less
• No pulse: cardiac arrest. CPR (cardiopulmonary resuscitation) and a shock
• Pulse but unstable (low BP, new confusion, chest pain, signs of shock, acute heart failure): synchronized cardioversion for monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, as ordered
• Pulse and stable: stay with him, pads on, 12-lead ECG (electrocardiogram), IV (intravenous) access, call. Antiarrhythmic as ordered

🧠 Ventricular tachycardia (RACE): too fast to fill. Pulse first.

memory_line: Pulseless electrical activity (EMPTY): the wires fire, the pump is empty.
caption_lesson:
✅ First, normal sinus rhythm
• One signal, one squeeze, one pulse. The chambers refill between beats

🔌 Then pulseless electrical activity (EMPTY)
1️⃣ The wiring still fires: P waves, QRS, T waves. The strip can look organized, even normal
2️⃣ But the pump moves too little blood to make a pulse. It's cardiac arrest
3️⃣ Why: no blood to pump, the heart squeezed or blocked, or a heart too sick to squeeze

⚡ What to do
• Not responding? Check breathing and the carotid (neck) pulse together, no more than 10 seconds
• No pulse: start CPR (cardiopulmonary resuscitation) right away
• NOT shockable
• Epinephrine as soon as possible, then every 3 to 5 minutes, as ordered

🔍 Find the cause: the Hs and Ts
• Hs: hypovolemia (low volume), hypoxia (low oxygen), hydrogen ion (acidosis), hypo-/hyperkalemia (low or high potassium), hypothermia
• Ts: tension pneumothorax, tamponade (cardiac), toxins, thrombosis (pulmonary, coronary)

🧠 Pulseless electrical activity (EMPTY): treat the patient, not the monitor.

caption_lesson:
🌙 Night shift, 2:05 AM. He's 71, panicking and pulling at his IV (intravenous) line.
• Order: midazolam 1 mg IV to calm him

❌ 3 mistakes
1️⃣ Took a vial from a leftover intubation kit
2️⃣ Mixed a powder and never read the cap warning
3️⃣ Lights off, door closed, no monitor
➡️ He can't move or breathe, and he's awake for it. Then the oxygen runs out. Code blue.

💉 Two drugs, two jobs

🟢 Midazolam (CALMS)
• A benzodiazepine (sedative): calms, makes sleepy
• Comes as a liquid
• Can slow breathing: monitor breathing and SpO2 (oxygen saturation) after IV doses

🔴 Vecuronium (STOPS THE BREATHING)
• A paralytic (neuromuscular blocker): stops every skeletal muscle, breathing included. The heart keeps beating until the oxygen runs out
• NO sedation, NO pain relief: the patient is awake and feels everything
• Comes as a powder. The cap must say "Warning: Paralyzing Agent". Read the words, not the color
• Only with sedation, airway control (breathing tube, ventilator) and trained staff

✅ The right move
• Give only the patient's own verified dose. Read the full label every time
• Mixing a powder for a drug that comes as a liquid? Stop. Wrong drug
• After any IV sedative: stay and monitor breathing and SpO2

hook: Nurses: QTc 560. Just a number on the strip?

memory_line: Torsades de pointes (TWIST): a long QT, then the twist.
caption_lesson:
✅ First, normal sinus rhythm
• QRS = the ventricles fire. T wave = they recover and reset
• QT = from the start of the QRS to the end of the T wave. QTc is the QT corrected for heart rate

🌀 Then torsades de pointes (TWIST)
1️⃣ The ventricles take too long to reset: a long QT
2️⃣ An early beat lands on that long T wave
3️⃣ The signal spins around the ventricles, changing direction. The QRS gets bigger, then smaller, twisting around the line
4️⃣ Twisting ventricles can't squeeze well. Short runs can stop on their own (dizzy, fainting), but it can lose its pulse or turn into ventricular fibrillation (QUIVER)

⚠️ What stretches the QT
• Drugs like ondansetron, haloperidol, some antibiotics, methadone
• Low potassium, low magnesium
• QTc over 500 ms (milliseconds): high risk. Report it

⚡ What to do
• Sustained torsades, even with a pulse: an unsynchronized shock (defibrillation), never synchronized cardioversion. No pulse: CPR (cardiopulmonary resuscitation) too
• Magnesium sulfate IV (intravenous), as ordered
• Stop the QT-prolonging drugs. Correct potassium and magnesium, as ordered

🌙 Night shift, 1:30 AM. She's 68, day 1 after a knee replacement.
• Takes sertraline (an SSRI, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor) every day
• New order: tramadol for pain
• Now: sweating, shivering, legs jerking. 38.9 °C (102 °F), heart rate 122

🔥 Two drug reactions, both with a high fever

⚡ Serotonin syndrome (FAST AND TWITCHY)
• Hours after starting or raising a serotonin drug: SSRIs, tramadol, linezolid, triptans and more
• Jerking muscles (clonus), tremor, shivering, sweating, diarrhea, agitation
• Stop the serotonin drugs, report now. Cooling, benzodiazepines, cyproheptadine, as ordered

🧊 Neuroleptic malignant syndrome, NMS (SLOW AND STIFF)
• Days to weeks after an antipsychotic like haloperidol
• Lead-pipe rigidity (stiff all over), slow responses, confusion
• Stop the antipsychotic, report now. Cooling, fluids, treatment as ordered

✅ The right move
• New fever with jerking or rigidity? Check the med list first
• Hold the trigger drug and call

memory_line: Third-degree AV block (SPLIT): the top and bottom beat apart.
caption_lesson:
✅ First, normal sinus rhythm
• Every P wave is followed by a QRS after the same short pause (PR 0.12 to 0.20 seconds)
• The AV (atrioventricular) node passes every signal

🧱 Then third-degree AV block (SPLIT), also called complete heart block
1️⃣ The AV node blocks EVERY signal. The atria (upper chambers) keep firing on time
2️⃣ A backup pacemaker below the block takes over, slowly: 40 to 60 from the junction (narrow QRS) or 20 to 40 from the ventricles (wide QRS)
3️⃣ Top and bottom SPLIT: P waves and QRS each march on their own clock. The PR changes every beat
4️⃣ Too slow to hold the BP (blood pressure). Dizziness, fainting, and the backup can fail

⚡ What to do
• Check her: pulse, BP, how she looks
• Pads on now. Atropine may be ordered first, but it often fails in third-degree block, so be ready for transcutaneous pacing (through the skin), as ordered
• Call now. A permanent pacemaker is the usual fix
